task: Reverse Sync + Preview: push a dbt result from the Warehouse back into a Postgres database, writing only in stage/prod and producing a Preview (what would change, without writing) in dev

analysis.objective: Add a Reverse Sync Step to adops Pipelines that copies a dbt model's rows from the Warehouse into an existing table of an operational Postgres database by key: it writes only when the Environment is named stage or prod, and in every other Environment it produces a Preview of the inserts, updates and deletes it would make. The demo Reverse Syncs a new per-customer dbt model customer_stats into shop.customer_stats, end to end on both Postgres and DuckDB Warehouses.
analysis.successDefinition: Done when ALL of these hold. (1) A Pipeline YAML can declare a Reverse Sync Step (e.g. `type: reverse_sync`) naming the dbt model, the target connection, the target table, a key column, a column mapping, an optional `delete_missing: true` and an optional max-change share. `adops validate` accepts a valid one and rejects a malformed one with a clear, sanitized error. (2) One pure domain function computes the diff (inserts, updates, deletes) from the dbt result rows and the target rows read by key. The Preview and the write both use that same diff object, and a unit test proves they cannot disagree. (3) One pure domain rule decides write vs Preview from the Environment name alone. Only `stage` and `prod` write; dev and any other name (including future Branch Environments) produce a Preview. No adops.yaml or Pipeline field can turn on writes elsewhere, and unit tests show this for dev, stage, prod and an arbitrary name. (4) In stage/prod, adops applies exactly the computed diff in ONE psycopg transaction. Any error rolls back the whole transaction, leaves the target unchanged and raises a fixed, sanitized error. Deletes run only when the table opts in with `delete_missing: true`. (5) The Preview writes nothing to the target. It prints counts of would-insert, would-update and would-delete (deletes are shown as 'would delete' only with the opt-in, otherwise as rows absent from the dbt result that will be kept), plus a bounded sample. (6) Built-in Checks guard every Reverse Sync. Each verdict comes from a pure domain rule over measured facts, and a failed Check fails the Step and stops every later Step. The Checks are: (a) the target table and mapped columns exist; (b) the key column is unique and never NULL in the dbt result; (c) the max-change guard stops the Step when updates plus deletes would exceed the configured share of target rows; (d) the dbt result is not empty. Each Check runs in both Preview and write mode, before anything is written. Skipping one needs `skip_checks` plus a non-empty reason where allowed, and `adops validate` lists every skip. (7) The demo seed SQL creates `customer_stats` in the demo shop Postgres. The demo dbt project adds a per-customer model `customer_stats` (customer_id, order_count, total_amount, last_order_at; no email) and the demo pipeline adds a Reverse Sync of it into the target table, keyed by customer_id. The demo adops.yaml ships a `stage` Environment next to dev (same containers, its own Warehouse location), and the demo scaffold tests (DEMO_FILES, .env.example, port checks) still pass. (8) The Docker E2E test proves, on both the Postgres and DuckDB Warehouse kinds, that `adops run --env dev` prints a Preview and leaves `customer_stats` unchanged, and that `adops run --env stage` writes the expected rows into `customer_stats`. It stays within the existing 20-minute CI timeout. (9) 100% line and branch coverage holds with no new `pragma: no cover`. The domain and application layers import no psycopg, dagster or os. No secret value appears in any output, log or error, as asserted by tests. ruff and `uv sync --locked` pass. (10) GLOSSARY.md defines Diff, Max-change guard and Reverse Sync target and says only stage and prod write.
assumptions: confirmed: Deletes: the default is insert + update only. A table opts in with `delete_missing: true` to also delete target rows missing from the dbt result. The Preview reports deletes either way, as 'would delete' only when opted in.

confirmed: Engine: adops computes the diff itself, reading dbt result rows from the Warehouse and target rows by key and computing inserts/updates/deletes. In stage/prod it applies exactly that diff in ONE transaction with psycopg, which is already a runtime dependency (psycopg[binary]>=3.3,<4). dlt is not used. Preview and write share the same diff.

confirmed: Demo target: the demo Reverse Syncs a NEW per-customer dbt model customer_stats (customer_id, order_count, total_amount, last_order_at; no email; user-confirmed after Discovery showed customer_orders is per-order and holds email) into a NEW table `customer_stats` in the existing demo shop Postgres, created by the demo seed SQL. No new container. adops never creates tables in an operational database.

confirmed: Write rule: a pure domain rule decides by Environment name. Only Environments named `stage` or `prod` write; every other name (dev, any future Branch Environment) produces a Preview. Nothing in adops.yaml can enable writes in dev.

confirmed: Built-in Checks guard every Reverse Sync in ADR-0013 style: (a) the target table and mapped columns exist; (b) the key column is unique and non-NULL in the dbt result; (c) a configurable max-change guard; (d) the dbt result is not empty. Verdicts come from pure domain rules over measured facts. A failed Check stops the Step and later Steps, and skipping one is allowed only with a written reason where applicable.

confirmed: The demo adops.yaml ships a `stage` Environment in addition to dev, using the same demo containers but its own Warehouse location, so `adops run --env stage` performs a real write. The Docker E2E proves Preview in dev (no write) and a write in stage on both the Postgres and DuckDB Warehouse kinds.

Assumed: the Reverse Sync Step runs after the Transform Step in linear YAML order (decision 2026-11-18). It reads the dbt model from the Transform's target schema (`analytics`), and an earlier failed Check already stops it.

Assumed: the stage Environment's 'own Warehouse location' is a separate Postgres database or schema in the same warehouse container (for example created by the compose init or seed) and a separate DuckDB file path for the DuckDB kind. Schema snapshots stay per-Environment in that location.

Assumed: the diff compares values after normalizing them to a canonical form (for example Decimal vs int/float, timezone-aware timestamps), so an unchanged row read from DuckDB or Postgres is never reported as an update.
Assumed: the full dbt result and the target key set fit in memory for v1-sized tables. The demo table is tiny.
Assumed: the stage write in the E2E is triggered by `adops run --env stage` run locally. GitHub Actions Promotion is not needed to reach stage.
confirmed: local dlt state (.adops/dlt) becomes per-Environment, folded into this horizon.
confirmed: a Postgres service is added to the CI unit job so the Reverse Sync writer's commit/rollback is unit-tested against real Postgres.
confirmed: Reverse Sync targets live in a new optional `targets` map on each Environment, not in `sources`.
confirmed: the max-change guard measures (updates + deletes) / target row count against max_change_share (default 0.5); an empty target table passes.
confirmed: the Preview sample shows at most 5 entries per kind (insert/update/delete): key values and changed column names only, never other values.
confirmed: the write re-reads target rows under SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside its one transaction and refuses to write (rolls back, fixed error) if the Diff no longer matches.
confirmed: writes_allowed is case-sensitive: only exactly 'stage' and 'prod' write.
confirmed: the horizon keeps all 7 phases and ends with the Docker E2E (user choice over the 3-5 soft target).
risks: Value normalization across Warehouse kinds: DuckDB and Postgres return different Python types for numeric, timestamp and boolean columns. A naive equality check reports every row as an update, which would trip the max-change guard and break the 'Preview equals write' promise.

Partial writes: if the diff is not applied in one transaction, or the connection drops mid-apply, the operational table could be left half-updated. Rollback must be tested against a real Postgres, not only fakes.

Read/write race: target rows changing between the diff read and the write make the applied diff stale. Without reading inside the write transaction (or with too weak an isolation level), updates could overwrite concurrent changes.

PII in output: the Preview sample and diff errors could print customer data from the operational database, against the horizon-3 precedent of never printing Source row values. The sample format has to be bounded and tested.
Secret safety: psycopg connection errors can echo host, user or DSN fragments. Target connect failures need fixed, sanitized messages like the Source/Warehouse unreachable errors.

Stage Environment wiring: giving stage its own Warehouse location in the same container may need compose/init SQL changes. It must keep the demo scaffold tests (DEMO_FILES exact match, .env.example vars, port checks) passing, and it must not break dbt-duckdb's process-wide DuckDB handle when one E2E process runs both Environments and both kinds.

Identifier safety: target table and column names come from YAML. They must be validated with the existing names rules and quoted with psycopg.sql, never string-formatted, or a malicious or typo'd name could inject SQL into an operational database.

E2E runtime and flakiness: adding dev + stage runs on two Warehouse kinds roughly doubles the current 92s scenario. That is still far under the 20-min timeout, but more output means more chances for flaky substring asserts (see the '999' in a Dagster run UUID).

Mapping the dbt result's column types onto pre-existing target column types (e.g. bigint vs numeric) may fail at write time even though the existence Check passed. A type-compatibility failure must surface as a clear sanitized error.
Coverage: 100% branch coverage on a transactional writer needs real-Postgres adapter tests (or a carefully shaped seam). Fakes alone would leave the rollback branches unproven.
outOfScope: Reverse Sync to SaaS destinations (CRMs, ad platforms, APIs): ADR-0003 limits v1 to database destinations.
Reverse Sync into non-Postgres operational databases (MySQL, SQL Server, DuckDB as a target): only Postgres is needed for the demo and v1 success criterion (2).
Creating or migrating target tables in the operational database: confirmed that adops never creates tables there; the user (or demo seed SQL) owns the schema.
Branch Environments (per-branch schemas, defer to stage, drop on merge): they get Preview behaviour for free through the name rule, but creating them is a later horizon.
GitHub Actions Promotion (PR to Branch Environment, merge to stage, release to prod) and a prod Environment in the demo: only `stage` is added to the demo. Promotion workflows are a later horizon.
MCP server tools (including a Preview tool) and the six Assistant skills: these are separate later horizons, and refusing stage/prod in MCP server code belongs there.
Using dlt or any third-party reverse-ETL engine for the write: confirmed that adops computes and applies the diff itself with psycopg.
Streaming/batched diffs for very large tables or incremental Reverse Sync by cursor: v1 diffs the full model in memory, which is enough for the demo. Scaling is deferred until a real need appears.
Soft deletes, upsert-only conflict strategies or per-column update policies beyond the key + mapped columns + delete_missing opt-in: these were not requested, and YAGNI applies.
Persisting Preview results (files, tables, PR comments) or a Preview-approval gate before writing: the Preview is printed to the run output only. Approval flows belong to Promotion.
Scheduling Reverse Sync runs: the open scheduling blocker (daemon vs cron/CI) is not resolved here.
Fixing the existing dbt source-test naming blocker or other open blockers not about Reverse Sync: unrelated to this horizon's objective.
analysis.domainShapeReason: The objective is about DataOps rules that a data-engineering expert would recognize: write only in stage/prod and Preview everywhere else, opt-in delete semantics, and Checks such as the max-change guard that stop a Step before it touches an operational database. It is not mainly about tooling machinery.

ubiquitousLanguage.meaning: A Pipeline Step that copies a dbt result from the Warehouse back into a table of an operational Postgres database, matched by a key column.
A Reverse Sync run that reports the inserts, updates and deletes it would make, plus a bounded sample, without writing anything. It happens in every Environment except stage and prod.
The set of inserts, updates and (opt-in) deletes computed by a pure domain rule from the dbt result rows and the target rows by key. The Preview reports it, and a write applies exactly it.
A fully separate place a Pipeline runs (dev, stage, prod) with its own Warehouse location and secrets. Its name alone decides whether a Reverse Sync writes or produces a Preview.
A fixed rule over measured facts that gives the same pass or fail for the same data. A failed Check fails its Step and stops every later Step, and skipping one needs a written reason.
A built-in Reverse Sync Check that stops the Step when the Diff would update or delete more than a configured share of the target rows.
The Postgres or DuckDB database where synced data and dbt results live, and where a Reverse Sync reads its rows from.
One unit of work inside a Pipeline (Sync, Transform or Reverse Sync), run in linear YAML order.

phases.name: Add Reverse Sync Step and targets to config

phases.rationale: Every later phase needs a typed, validated description of a Reverse Sync (which dbt model, which target table, which key, which columns) and of where the target database lives. phases.name: Add Diff, write rule and Reverse Sync Checks
phases.goal: Provide one pure function that computes the Diff (inserts, updates and opt-in deletes) between the dbt result rows and the target rows by key, one pure rule that decides from the Environment name alone whether a Reverse Sync writes or produces a Preview, and the pure verdict rules of the five built-in Reverse Sync Checks.
phases.rationale: The Preview (what would change, without writing) and the real write must never disagree, so both come from the same Diff value computed in one place. Only Environments named exactly `stage` or `prod` may write, and the repo requires Check verdicts to be pure rules over measured facts, so the write rule and the Checks (duplicate keys, empty result, a Diff that would rewrite most of the table) live in pure domain code that nothing in configuration can switch off.
changes: Create src/adops/domain/reverse_sync_diff.py with a frozen Diff dataclass holding inserts, updates (key, changed column names, new values) and deletes (keys), and a delete_missing flag that says whether deletes will be applied or only reported as rows that are kept.

Add compute_diff(result_rows, target_rows, key, mapping, delete_missing) -> Diff. Rename dbt result columns to target columns through the mapping before comparing; treat target rows missing from the result as deletes only when delete_missing is true, otherwise record them as 'absent from the dbt result, kept'.

Add normalize_value used on both sides before comparison: numerically equal Decimal/int/float compare equal, naive and timezone-aware timestamps are compared in UTC, booleans stay booleans, so an unchanged row read from DuckDB or Postgres is never reported as an update.

Add preview_sample(diff, limit) returning, per kind (insert/update/delete), at most `limit` entries containing only the key value and, for updates, the changed column NAMES, never other column values.

Add writes_allowed(environment_name: str) -> bool returning True only for exactly 'stage' or 'prod' (case-sensitive), so 'dev', 'Stage', 'PROD' and any future Branch Environment name produce a Preview.

In src/adops/domain/checks.py add a frozen ReverseSyncFacts dataclass (target table exists, missing target column names, result row count, duplicate key count, NULL key count, target row count, Diff update and delete counts) and evaluate_reverse_sync(step, facts) -> tuple[CheckResult, ...], reusing CheckResult and SkipChecks (a skipped Check is reported with its written reason).

Check rules: max_change fails when (updates + deletes) / target row count exceeds step.max_change_share (deletes count only with delete_missing; an empty target passes so the first stage write is allowed); result_not_empty fails on zero rows; key_unique / key_not_null fail on any duplicate or NULL key; target_columns_exist fails when the table or any mapped column is missing (text names columns, never row values).

Unit-test: insert/update/delete detection, delete_missing on and off, Decimal-vs-float and naive-vs-aware rows reported unchanged, bounded key-only sample, writes_allowed for dev, stage, prod, 'Stage' and an arbitrary name, and each Check rule at its boundary (exactly at the share, just over, empty target) plus skipped-with-reason.

In GLOSSARY.md add the terms Diff, Max-change guard and Reverse Sync target (the operational Postgres table a Reverse Sync writes to), and state under Preview that only the stage and prod Environments write.

rubric.label: writes_allowed is true only for exactly 'stage' and 'prod'

rubric.label: Equal values from DuckDB or Postgres never produce updates
rubric.ruleStatement: compute_diff normalizes both sides through normalize_value so numerically equal Decimal/int/float, and naive vs UTC-aware timestamps of the same instant, compare equal, while genuinely different values and booleans are still detected correctly.
passCriteria: A test with result row total_amount=Decimal('10.50') and target row total_amount=10.5 (float) yields zero updates.
A test with a naive datetime vs the same instant as a tz-aware UTC datetime yields zero updates; a test with a tz-aware non-UTC timestamp representing the same instant also yields zero updates.
A test asserts True vs 1 is NOT silently treated as unchanged when the target column is boolean, or documents and tests the chosen rule (booleans stay booleans).
A test with a real value change (e.g. order_count 3 -> 4) yields exactly one update listing only `order_count` as changed column.
failureExamples: normalize_value converts everything to float, so Decimal('0.1')+Decimal('0.2') and 0.3 compare unequal or large Decimals lose precision.
Naive timestamps are compared directly to aware ones, raising TypeError or reporting every row as updated.
The update entry lists all mapped columns instead of only the changed ones.

rubric.label: Deletes are applied only with delete_missing; mapping renames before comparing
rubric.ruleStatement: Target rows absent from the dbt result appear as deletes to apply only when delete_missing is true and are otherwise recorded as 'absent from the dbt result, kept'; comparisons use target column names after applying the mapping.
passCriteria: A test with delete_missing=False and one target-only key asserts the Diff marks it as kept (not to be deleted) and the Diff's delete_missing flag is False.
The same fixture with delete_missing=True asserts exactly that key is a delete.
A test where the mapping renames a result column (e.g. orders -> order_count) asserts the comparison uses the target name and produces no spurious insert/update.
Diff is a frozen dataclass (assigning to a field raises FrozenInstanceError in a test).
failureExamples: Target-only rows are dropped from the Diff entirely when delete_missing is false, so the Preview cannot report them.
The mapping is applied to result rows but target rows are read with result-side names, so every row looks like an insert.

rubric.label: Preview sample carries keys and column names only, bounded per kind
rubric.ruleStatement: preview_sample(diff, limit) returns at most `limit` entries per kind, each containing only the key value and, for updates, the changed column NAMES — never any other column value.
passCriteria: A test with 12 inserts, 12 updates and 12 deletes and limit=5 asserts exactly 5 entries per kind.
A test builds rows whose non-key values are sentinel strings (e.g. 'SENTINEL_VALUE') and asserts repr(preview_sample(...)) does not contain the sentinel.
Update entries expose changed column names (e.g. ('order_count',)) and no old/new values.
failureExamples: Update sample entries include new values 'to be helpful', leaking amounts into CLI output.
The limit is applied to the total across kinds instead of per kind, so deletes never appear when there are many inserts.
The sample order is set-iteration order, so tests pass locally but the sample is non-deterministic.

rubric.label: Reverse Sync Check verdicts are exact at their boundaries
rubric.ruleStatement: evaluate_reverse_sync(step, facts) returns one CheckResult per Reverse Sync Check from ReverseSyncFacts alone, with max_change = (updates + counted deletes) / target rows > max_change_share failing, an empty target passing, and skipped Checks reported with their reason.
passCriteria: Tests in tests/unit/domain/test_checks.py cover max_change exactly at the share (passes), one row over (fails), an empty target with inserts only (passes), and deletes counted only when delete_missing is true.

Tests cover result_not_empty on 0 rows, key_unique with 1 duplicate, key_not_null with 1 NULL, and target_columns_exist with a missing table and with a missing mapped column; failure text names columns but no row values.
A test asserts a skipped Check yields a CheckResult marked skipped carrying the step's written reason.
evaluate_reverse_sync performs no I/O and takes no adapter or connection parameter.
failureExamples: max_change uses >= so a Diff exactly at max_change_share fails.
Empty target divides by zero or fails max_change, blocking the very first stage write.
Deletes are counted in max_change even when delete_missing is false, failing a run that would delete nothing.

phases.healerHint: The most likely failure is phantom updates from Decimal-vs-float or naive-vs-aware timestamps (or an off-by-one at max_change_share); fix by normalizing both sides to Decimal/UTC in normalize_value and using a strict > comparison, with a boundary test for each.

phases.name: Add Reverse Sync Step to the run plan
phases.goal: Let run_pipeline plan and run a Reverse Sync Step through a new ReverseSync port: resolve the target connection's secret, measure facts, run the Checks, then either return a Preview or ask the engine to apply exactly the computed Diff, with fixed sanitized errors and later Steps stopped on failure.
phases.rationale: The use case is where the pure rules meet the outside world: it decides write vs Preview with writes_allowed, runs the Checks before anything is written, and turns engine failures into fixed messages that never leak a password. Add TargetUnreachable and WriteFailed marker exceptions. successCriteria: Done when ALL of these hold. (1) A Pipeline YAML can declare a Reverse Sync Step (e.g. `type: reverse_sync`) naming the dbt model, the target connection, the target table, a key column, a column mapping, an optional `delete_missing: true` and an optional max-change share. `adops validate` accepts a valid one and rejects a malformed one with a clear, sanitized error. (2) One pure domain function computes the diff (inserts, updates, deletes) from the dbt result rows and the target rows read by key. The Preview and the write both use that same diff object, and a unit test proves they cannot disagree. (3) One pure domain rule decides write vs Preview from the Environment name alone. Only `stage` and `prod` write; dev and any other name (including future Branch Environments) produce a Preview. No adops.yaml or Pipeline field can turn on writes elsewhere, and unit tests show this for dev, stage, prod and an arbitrary name. (4) In stage/prod, adops applies exactly the computed diff in ONE psycopg transaction. Any error rolls back the whole transaction, leaves the target unchanged and raises a fixed, sanitized error. Deletes run only when the table opts in with `delete_missing: true`. (5) The Preview writes nothing to the target. It prints counts of would-insert, would-update and would-delete (deletes are shown as 'would delete' only with the opt-in, otherwise as rows absent from the dbt result that will be kept), plus a bounded sample. (6) Built-in Checks guard every Reverse Sync. Each verdict comes from a pure domain rule over measured facts, and a failed Check fails the Step and stops every later Step. The Checks are: (a) the target table and mapped columns exist; (b) the key column is unique and never NULL in the dbt result; (c) the max-change guard stops the Step when updates plus deletes would exceed the configured share of target rows; (d) the dbt result is not empty. Each Check runs in both Preview and write mode, before anything is written. Skipping one needs `skip_checks` plus a non-empty reason where allowed, and `adops validate` lists every skip. (7) The demo seed SQL creates `customer_stats` in the demo shop Postgres. The demo dbt project adds a per-customer model `customer_stats` (customer_id, order_count, total_amount, last_order_at; no email) and the demo pipeline adds a Reverse Sync of it into the target table, keyed by customer_id. The demo adops.yaml ships a `stage` Environment next to dev (same containers, its own Warehouse location), and the demo scaffold tests (DEMO_FILES, .env.example, port checks) still pass. (8) The Docker E2E test proves, on both the Postgres and DuckDB Warehouse kinds, that `adops run --env dev` prints a Preview and leaves `customer_stats` unchanged, and that `adops run --env stage` writes the expected rows into `customer_stats`. It stays within the existing 20-minute CI timeout. (9) 100% line and branch coverage holds with no new `pragma: no cover`. The domain and application layers import no psycopg, dagster or os. No secret value appears in any output, log or error, as asserted by tests. ruff and `uv sync --locked` pass. (10) GLOSSARY.md defines Diff, Max-change guard and Reverse Sync target and says only stage and prod write.

deferred: Reverse Sync to SaaS destinations (CRMs, ad platforms, APIs): ADR-0003 limits v1 to database destinations.
Reverse Sync into non-Postgres operational databases (MySQL, SQL Server, DuckDB as a target): only Postgres is needed for the demo and v1 success criterion (2).
Creating or migrating target tables in the operational database: confirmed that adops never creates tables there; the user (or demo seed SQL) owns the schema.
Branch Environments (per-branch schemas, defer to stage, drop on merge): they get Preview behaviour for free through the name rule, but creating them is a later horizon.
GitHub Actions Promotion (PR to Branch Environment, merge to stage, release to prod) and a prod Environment in the demo: only `stage` is added to the demo. Promotion workflows are a later horizon.
MCP server tools (including a Preview tool) and the six Assistant skills: these are separate later horizons, and refusing stage/prod in MCP server code belongs there.
Using dlt or any third-party reverse-ETL engine for the write: confirmed that adops computes and applies the diff itself with psycopg.
Streaming/batched diffs for very large tables or incremental Reverse Sync by cursor: v1 diffs the full model in memory, which is enough for the demo. Scaling is deferred until a real need appears.
Soft deletes, upsert-only conflict strategies or per-column update policies beyond the key + mapped columns + delete_missing opt-in: these were not requested, and YAGNI applies.
Persisting Preview results (files, tables, PR comments) or a Preview-approval gate before writing: the Preview is printed to the run output only. Approval flows belong to Promotion.
Scheduling Reverse Sync runs: the open scheduling blocker (daemon vs cron/CI) is not resolved here.
Fixing the existing dbt source-test naming blocker or other open blockers not about Reverse Sync: unrelated to this horizon's objective.
A generic connection-factory seam so the writer can be tested with fake DB-API connections: fails YAGNI gate 4 (the CI Postgres service gives real commit/rollback tests).
